utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number case IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know if I am expected to switch on to French but I am receiving interpretation in French on channel 4 so there is something wrong there, too. Oh, it has gone to channel 3 now? Yes. Let's go through it again. I am not receiving interpretation in French now so it should be okay. Mr. Jones and Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I was receiving in French but I'm getting English now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: It's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Mr. Oric, good morning to you, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am receiving the interpretation in my own language, and I can hear you perfectly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Now there is something wrong. I did not receive any interpretation in English at all and I am on channel 3. I should switch now to channel 4? Yes, again I have to ask you again, Mr. Oric because I want to make sure that there is nothing wrong with interpretation on your side. Are you receiving interpretation in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes, I am receiving the interpretation in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning to you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, and also good morning to my learned friends of the Defence. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. I'm here together with co-counsel, Ms. Patricia Sellers, Ms. Joanne Richardson, and our case manager, Mrs. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my learned colleagues from the OTP. My name is Vasvija Vidovic and together with Mr. John Jones I appear for Mr. Naser Oric. And we have here with us our legal assistants, Miss Jasmina Cosic, and our CaseMap manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning to your team. Any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My apologies for starting with a few minutes' delay. The problem was traffic jams this morning. I simply don't know what happened, but I would have made it earlier had I walked from my residence to the Tribunal and the same applies to my colleagues. So, let's bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, to you, Mr. Sacirovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome to this Tribunal. You are about to start giving evidence. Before you do so, our rules require that you enter a -- you make a solemn declaration equivalent to an oath in some jurisdictions. Since that, in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is contained in a piece of paper which the usher is going to hand to you now. Please read it out loud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will throughout the proceedings be receiving interpretation from what will be said in English into your own language. If at any time there are problems with reception of interpretation, please draw our attention straight away. I am the Presiding Judge in this case. My name is Carmel Agius and I come from Malta. To my right I have Judge Hans Henrik Brydensholt from the Kingdom of Denmark, to my left, Judge Professor Albin Eser from Germany. The procedure is Defence will go first with asking you a series of questions because you are a Defence witness. Later on, you will be

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And good morning from me, Mr. Sacirovic.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If we could start with you, please, giving the Court your full name.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. What is it, please, your full name?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: My name is Mustafa, my last name is Sacirovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Please confirm the following details: You were born on the 1st of April, 1953 in Hranca, Bratunac municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You went to primary school in Bratunac, graduating in 1968?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You completed higher education in catering and tourism in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You moved to Glogova in 1971?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And before the war, you worked as a trader or as a waiter?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And after the war, you moved to Portland, Oregon, in the United States?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you undertake or complete any training in the United States?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What training did you undertake?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: I graduated from the school for private investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So in other words you trained as a private investigator?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in Portland, you have a registered centre of investigation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the investigation centre of the victims of genocide of Bosnia-Herzegovina. IMSGS.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter isn't certain about the abbreviation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could you tell us again the abbreviation for your centre?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: ICGS. Therefore, no S in the abbreviation. It's the letter C.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fine. In fact, is it right that the full title is "The Union of Victims of Genocide of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Enclave of Srebrenica, Centre of Investigation, Portland?"

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And as part of your activities for that centre, have you collected tapes, testimonies, and exhibits relating to events in Bosnia in 1992 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you give those statements and testimonies to the state commission on war crimes in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And have you also given a statement as well as provided other witness statements and audiotapes to the Prosecutor of this Tribunal in regard to the Deronjic case?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, for the purposes of your testimony, we are not going to dwell on ethnic cleansing in Bratunac, Srebrenica, in early 1992, since the Judges have indicated they've heard enough evidence on that subject. I simply want to show you an exhibit which is D89.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown D89, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally, while this is being transported, we -- none of us has the documents relating to -- the documents that you will be using because we only got the list this morning, just before the sitting actually, so our secretaries have not been in a position to prepare anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I think there were some technical --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not criticising you. I mean, so it's important that we either have the cooperation of the Prosecution to have the documents available on Sanction, or the Defence, or else to make sure that it is always -- that they are always placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour -- Good morning to Your Honour and to the Defence. Your Honour, we, just as you have, received the list this morning. We have not had time to prepare, so I'm sorry we can't assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll see, we'll play it by the ear as we go along.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There might be problems. It's important that we have it on the ELMO at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to say for the record in any event that we did send it out last night and, as I say, there must be a technical hitch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm told so, so much so. I told you I'm not blaming you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I just thought I should state that anyway. And we don't use Sanction so it will be a question of using the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, this exhibit, just for the record as well, it has the name Mustafa Sacirovic at the top left-hand corner and then the address of the International Criminal Tribunal. I'd ask you firstly, did you prepare this document?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And is it your signature at the end of this document?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And is it also signed as being received by an investigator of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, are the contents of this document true to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you prepare it with the benefit of testimonies of people who survived these events?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you therefore vouch for what is stated here about mass killings and expulsions in May 1992 in the following places in Bratunac municipality? And I'm going to, just for the record, read the names of the places: Hranca, Glogova, Bljeceva, Suha, Mihajlovici, Krasan Polje, Bratunac, in particular in the Vuk Karadzic school, Podcaus, Boljevici Zaluzje, Abdulici, Bjelovac, Zapolje, and Tegari? Do you vouch for what's stated here on ethnic cleansing of Muslims from all those villages?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: As a result of these events as described in this document, were all or practically all of the Muslims expelled from Bratunac municipality in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Most of them were. The majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And only if you can assist with this before we move on to looking at the document, do you have any explanation of how such massive crimes could be committed in such a wide area in such a short time?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: You have to know that the paramilitary units from Serbia had to do with this, the regular Yugoslav People's Army, and the local Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In your opinion, was this something that was organised or not organised?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: It was an organised action.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In terms of the victims mentioned in this document, are they the -- is this a list that's exhaustive or is it simply the victims you know about?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Listed here are the victims who I know, but this is not a final list of victims. The only possibility is that some of the victims were left out here, but I rule out the possibility of someone being listed here as a victim without being so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So in short there could be more victims than this but certainly not less?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your centre for investigating genocide in Portland, is that dealing only with events in 1995 or does it also deal with events beforehand?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Our centre deals with the events starting from 1992 throughout the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So your conclusion is that the genocide referred to in the title of your centre actually occurred before 1995?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When would you say it started, this genocide?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: The genocide started in May 1992 and it was prepared in April and probably even earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'm just going to go to a few parts of this document. First of all the section dealing with Hranca.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If we could put that on the ELMO, it's pages 1 to 3 of English and pages 1 to 2 in the Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: First of all, can I ask did you in fact grow up in Hranca?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was that a Muslim village or a Serb village or a mixed village before the war?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: It was a mixed village but the majority were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know Najdan Mladjenovic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before the war, he used to drive together with my brother. They were drivers before my brother was killed on the 9th of May. They were haulers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But where was your brother killed on the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: He was killed in Glogova, in our family house.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Going back to Najdan Mladjenovic, do you know where he's from?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: From Hranca.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And -- right. Okay. Now, according to this document, Najdan Mladjenovic was involved in crimes in Hranca on both the 3rd of May 1992 and the 9th of May 1992, and I'm just going to read a section from the top of page 2 of the English, where referring to the 3rd of May 1992, it says, "Soon after, at about 1500 hours on the same day, the Bosniak village of Hranca was surrounded on all sides. In this massacre, the SDS paramilitary formations killed," then there is a list, "Bego [phoen] Hodzic, Osman Ramic, Sancir Ramic, and Selma Hodzic, a girl of between five and seven. Between 40 and 50 Bosniak houses were torched in this bloody raid. The SDS Chetnik paramilitary formations were led in this bloody raid by the following who were seen at the scene," and it says Najdan Mladjenovic from Donji Magasici. I'll pause there for a moment. Is Donji Magasici in the Hranca area, or is that a separate village?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Donji Magasici is in the area of Hranca. Some consider it to be a distinct village but it is a part of Hranca.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. So according to the information which you collected, Najdan Mladjenovic led this raid on the 3rd of May 1992 when these people were killed and these houses were torched?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then when we go to the raid or the crime on the 9th of May 1992, and it's the same page in English, bottom paragraph, it says, "In this second raid on the defenceless Bosniak village of Hranca, a group of these SDS paramilitary formations led by Najdan Mladjenovic liquidated the men fit for military service and finally expelled the women and children towards Kladanj and Tuzla." Can you confirmed that that's the information you received about the 9th of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then finally, I just want to turn before moving to another document, on page 3 of the English, and the end of the first paragraph, it says, "It would not hurt to note that in the second raid the village of Hranca was completely torched and destroyed." Is that true, that Hranca was the Bosniak houses in Hranca were burned on the 9th of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know who was involved in those torchings?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: According to witness statements, Najdan Mladjenovic and others mentioned in these witness statements took part in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you have witness statements and audiotapes relating to the involvement of Najdan Mladjenovic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The tapes were handed over to The Hague investigator in Tuzla in 2000, I believe it was. It was a tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If you can keep D89 with you for the moment, I'd like to show the witness P487 which is also P294. And this is a -- it's entitled "report." And it concerns damage allegedly caused during combat activities in Eastern Bosnia and it's particularly the table which I want to ask you about. There is a table which in English it says "table overview of documented facilities burned and destroyed during military actions of 1992-1993." I don't know if you see that in Bosnian. In fact it's just the second page of the Bosnian. And if you look down to number 16 of the album, we see the information supplied about properties in Hranca, is Najdan Mladjenovic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is there more than one Najdan Mladjenovic living in the Hranca area?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would you say this is the Najdan Mladjenovic who you told us burnt Muslim homes in Hranca?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would you consider Najdan Mladjenovic a reliable, objective source on who damaged property in Hranca during the war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes? We don't -- we are not seeing anything on the ELMO so we don't really know which document -- is it P487, 294?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, P487 it's the second page in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's also P294.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher could you please put page 2 of that document, the English version?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: This is number 16, if we could get 16 in range. We need to raise it a bit higher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have to raise it a bit higher.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The other way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No that's -- okay. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If you left it as it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. No, further up.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. And now move it the other direction, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You had it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You had it before, usher. Why so much complication with something that is very simple?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, leave it there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Leave it. Yes, Ms. Richardson?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I would object to the last question being put to the witness about whether or not this individual is reliable unless this witness is capable or competent to testify that he spoke to the individual in question and I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But then you ask him on cross-examination if you contest it. I mean, he's got every right to ask him that question and if you don't like the answer or you want further explanation on the grounds for his answer, you ask him later.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I will do so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, let's not waste time because we are already ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question, Mr. Sacirovic, if I need to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would you consider Najdan Mladjenovic, a reliable, objective source on what caused damage to property in Hranca during the war?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And why not?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Because Najdan Mladjenovic participated in the destruction of Bosnian homes and the liquidation of the Bosniaks in the area, and I personally, as an investigator, believe that he cannot be a reliable person or, rather, his figures, the information provided by him, cannot be deemed accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know how many Muslim houses were actually burned in May 1992 in Hranca?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: All the houses were burnt down, and to obtain the data one needs only to look at the 1991 census data wherein in the exact numbers of the homes were listed, but, in any case, all the houses, all of them, were razed down, burnt down.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just roughly what number would that be, if you can attach a number?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: I believe that more than 100 houses were torched. Take a few, add a few, but anyway, I believe when we know what we have Cerovac [phoen], Mjelomina [phoen], Ramici, and the lower part of Polje, four hamlets making all part of Hranca.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we are going to go back to D89 again, that's your document, and turn to Glogova, which is page 3 of the English. Firstly, you've confirmed the accuracy of this document as a whole. Do you confirm what's stated here about Glogova being attacked, homes being burned, and a great many of its inhabitants being killed by the Serbs on the 9th of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: I do. I was in Glogova on the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In this document, we see the names of some of the Serb perpetrators and participants in this crime. It's on page 4 of the English, page 3 of the B/C/S. And it -- probably should get that on the ELMO for the record. Yes, that's probably -- that's fine, if you just leave it there. Now, without going through all the names, we see that there are Serbs from Kravica, Hranca, Donja Magasici. Is it true that many of the Serbs who participated in killing and burnings in Glogova in May 1992 were from the Kravica area?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So as early as May 1992, Serbs from Kravica and local Serbs were killing and raping their Muslim neighbours; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, let's turn to just a couple more entries. It's not possible to go through the whole document. For Voljavica and Zaluzje it's page 12 of the English, page 9 of the Bosnian. I'm going to read part of this. "Crime in the villages of Voljavica and Zaluzje on 13 May 1992. On 13 May 1992, the Bosniak villages of Voljavica and Zaluzje were surrounded by Bratunac SDS paramilitary units. Voljavica and Zaluzje are three kilometres to the east of Bratunac in the direction of Fakovici. On this occasion too the SDS goal was achieved and most of the people of these villages were expelled in buses and lorries towards Bratunac and then Kladanj and Tuzla. Both villages," that's Voljavica and Zaluzje, "were torched to a large extent and the following civilians were killed on the spot. And then there is a list of names. And the next paragraph, list of 12 names. The following SDS supporters were identified at the scene of the crime, if we go to the very bottom, we see Slavko Rankic from Bjelovac and others. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would it be right that this name, Slavko Rankic from Bjelovac, like the names of the other perpetrators and participants in these events appears in this document because eyewitnesses who survived the events named him or identified him?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was recognised on the spot and his name is on the list on the basis of witness statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you, as a matter of practice, check witness statements against each other, cross-reference them and check that the information is reliable?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. I always use several sources of information to arrive at the actual truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. If we turn back to P487, if that's still there, and it's that same page, and we look at item number 11, and we see there, do we not, that Slavko Rankic is a source of information on damage and destroyed property in Bjelovac. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. This document, this table, appears to rely, does it not, on information from Serbs who were actually implicated in the crimes of ethnic cleansing in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Turning back to your document it's page 13 of the English -- of the English version, page 10 of the B/C/S, refers to crime in the villages of Abdulici, Bjelovac, Zapolje, and Tegari, between 16 May and 20 May 1992 and again for the record, I'm going to read part of it. "The villages of Bjelovac, Tegari, and Zapolje lie along the River Drina to the east of Bratunac, like the village of Abdulici with its majority Bosniak population. On 16 May 1992, the villages of Tegari and Zapolje and the Roma settlement of Orlica was surrounded by Bratunac SDS paramilitary units. On the same day, the following were killed with firearms at the scene of the crime," and then there are some names of those who were killed. "The villages were completely torched and the people fled to the forest in the free territory of Srebrenica municipality. The following Serbs from Fakovici led by the SDS leadership of the local commune, Slavko Jovanovic, were recognised at the scene of the crime. Tihomir Jovanovic from Orlica, Vidoje Maksimovic from Fakovici, Ognjen Markovic, a.k.a. Bato, Milenko Canic, Dane Katanic, and Desimir Mitrovic, all from Fakovici and the surrounding area." And then it's mentioned, "the following were witnesses to this crime and the names Ednen Zildzic and Sadeta Zildzic." Now, did you take statements from Ednen Zildzic and Sadeta Zildzic about these events?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, we didn't have interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer, please? Could you repeat your last answer, Mr. Sacirovic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The English booth apologises. We were on the wrong channel. Answer: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. So that's yes you took the statements of these witnesses Ednen Zildzic and Sadeta Zildzic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you give those statements to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: I think it was in Tuzla in the year 2000. Together with those microcassettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So more than five years ago you gave statements from these witnesses about Serbs from Fakovici committing crimes in Abdulici, Bjelovac, Zapolje and Tegari?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Finally let's go to the last page of this document. It's page 15 in English. And I read, "However, in its attempt to take control of these parts, the SDS and its paramilitary units made new victims of the Bosniak people. In their attempt to ethnically cleanse the villages of Joseva and Jagodnja on the 14th of May 1992 they killed the following civilians in Joseva. Sacir Ibrahimovic and Hasib Kurtic who were killed in their village. In a repeated attempt on 22 May 1992, the following civilians were killed in Joseva: Rukija Paraganlija, Safija Paraganlija, Amira Paraganlija," -- sorry, Amira, that was, Paraganlija, "Amir Paraganlija, Fehim Dugonjic, Mustafa Dugonjic, Sefik," possibly Ketonic, "and Zineta Paraganlija, a pregnant woman. All those civilians killed were from Joseva. The following are surviving witnesses to the crime. Ibro Alic from Joseva, Bratunac Municipality, currently living in the Sarajevo area and Junuz Smajlovic from Joseva, Bratunac Municipality, currently living in the Osgova refugee settlement, Zivinice Municipality, and others." Now, would it be right to read this to mean that Ibro Alic and others provided you with information regarding these crimes committed by Serb forces in Jagodnja and Joseva in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And that that information implicated the SDS and paramilitary units referred to at the start of that paragraph in those crimes?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you provide that information to the investigator of the Tribunal in July 2000?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: I provided that information. However, there were statements I took when I was in Srebrenica in 1992, 1993, and right up to 1995, which I provided to the president of the War Presidency, Mr. Hajrudin Avdic. However, all this documentation remained in Srebrenica and I don't know what happened to it, if the Serbs didn't find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. We will come to that in a moment. Finally, Miroslav Deronjic you may know has been convicted by this Tribunal only in relation to events in Glogova. According to this document, and your information, was he only involved in events of ethnic cleansing in Glogova or in a broader area?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Miroslav Deronjic is responsible not only for the crimes in Glogova but for all the crimes, all over Bratunac municipality, throughout 1992 and later.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I've finished with those two documents. You've mentioned how your brother was killed by the Serbs in Glogova in May 1992. Were any of your other family members killed by the Serbs, firstly in Hranca in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Over 20 members of my family were killed in Hranca and my father was killed in Glogova on the 9th of May as well as my brother Vahid, Mehmed, my uncle Mujo, and not to enumerate them further, many, many members of my family were killed, because my mother originates from Glogova and my father from Hranca.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: As a result of those tragedies, did you start to collect information on war crimes?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as Glogova fell, as soon as there was an attack on Glogova, I managed to pull out to survive, and I immediately grabbed a pencil and started noting down events, who was killed, where, when, by whom, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And it may be an obvious question, but why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: I did that simply so that it would not be forgotten. I hoped if I was killed somebody would find those documents and would know that these events took place on those dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And how did you collect information?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Mostly from surviving witnesses. If I was unable to go to the scene and establish what happened, I collected information from more than one witness, compared the information, and then came to the conclusion that what they were saying was true.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And where did you go after Glogova fell on the 9th of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: I managed to break through and get to the village of Pale in Srebrenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you continue or not your activities of taking statements and collecting information on war crimes when you were in Pale?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was there a group of fighters in Pale in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did they have a leader of sorts?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Their leader was Mirzet Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was Mirzet Halilovic under any higher command at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: No. Mirzet Halilovic acted independently.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So what was the status of his group of fighters in Pale?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: It was a self-organised group without any particular status. How can I explain this? As far as military matters go, they didn't have anything to do with any kind of army. It was a self-organised group. They did what they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, at some stage, did you go on to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Sometime in early July, I received a message from the president of the War Presidency, Mr. Hajrudin Avdic, telling me to report urgently to Srebrenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And why did Hajrudin Avdic summon you in particular?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: When I got there, he told me he had heard I was writing down and collecting information about events on the ground, that is war crimes that happened on the ground. He knew I had come from Glogova and that I was writing this down, so he wanted to appoint me to the commission for the collecting of facts about war crimes. And that is how I began working in the war crimes commission attached to the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. And you mentioned Hajrudin Avdic as the president of the War Presidency. When you an arrived in Srebrenica in early July 1992, was the War Presidency already established?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Now, was anyone else from Pale summoned to Srebrenica by the War Presidency at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mirzet Halilovic was also summoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know what he was summoned to do?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: He had already been appointed commander of the military police, the War Presidency had appointed him, as a komandir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did Mirzet Halilovic in fact go to Srebrenica to take up that appointment?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He went there on the same day, took up his duties, and started working as some kind of military police commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, did Hajrudin Avdic have any sort of office in Srebrenica when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. His office was in the Srebrenica municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. And did you go to that building?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did go to that building. Hajrudin Avdic handed me a decision which said that I was the president of the commission for the gathering of facts about war crimes, which was attached to the service for communications and information.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And that service for communication and information, what organ did that belong to?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: It belonged to the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, did you subsequently have an office to work from?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had an office on the second floor, where the office of Mr. Hajrudin Avdic, president of the War Presidency, was also located. We were on the same floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did the War Presidency have meetings?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And where were those meetings held?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: In the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: From working on the same floor as Hajrudin Avdic, where he had his office, did you find out about the War Presidency and its members?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I knew that apart from Hajrudin Avdic, the president, there was also Hamdija Fejzic, the president of the executive council, Dzemal Becirevic, who was the chief for the economy. Then there was the chief of the civilian and military police, Becir Bogilovic, and there were some other people who were members on the ground and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. I want to ask you about Becir Bogilovic who you've described as the chief of the civilian and military police. From what period, as far as you were concerned, was he the chief of the civilian and military police?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Becir Bogilovic was chief of the civilian and military police until he left Srebrenica. This was until the end of 1992, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when you arrived in Srebrenica in early July 1992, was he already in that position or did he take that position later?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: No. He was already in that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, why do you say that he was the head of the civilian and military police from July 1992 until the end of 1992 or until he left Srebrenica? Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I say that because occasionally I saw him bringing in reports in the morning to Mr. Hajrudin Avdic, the president of the War Presidency, true to say he didn't come often. He had been wounded. Mirzet Halilovic and Nurija Jusufovic came more often. The former was a commander of the military police and the latter was commander of the civilian police, and both were subordinated to Becir Bogilovic. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know who subsequently succeeded Becir Bogilovic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Becir Bogilovic, when he left, was succeeded, I think, by Atif Krzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We are going to come to that in a moment. It's simply this: You say that Becir Bogilovic was chief of the civilian and military police until he left Srebrenica. "This was until the end of 1992, as far as I can recall." Are you sure about that date, end of 1992, or could it be either earlier or later?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: It was in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, where did the civilian police work?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: The civilian and the military police worked in the same building. The former building of the police station in Srebrenica. They were under the same roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is that what's also called the SUP or the MUP building?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I think you've told us -- well, let me ask: Did you see Becir Bogilovic at the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did. I just mentioned a while ago he didn't come often, but he did. I would see him when I was handing in my reports to the president of the War Presidency, Mr. Avdic. He would also bring in his reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And he would be bringing his reports to whom?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: He brought his reports to Hajrudin Avdic, the president of the War Presidency, just as I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you've also mentioned that Mirzet Halilovic and someone else came more often. Who was the other name which you mentions with Mirzet Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Nurija Jusufovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what was his function again?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Nurija Jusufovic was commander, that is komandir of the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to come to him in a moment but I want to stick with Mirzet Halilovic for a bit longer. Did Mirzet Halilovic make reports to the president of the War Presidency in this period from July 1992 onwards?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He came often, together with Nurija. Sometimes all three of them would come along, Becir, Nurija and Mirzet, but most often it was Mirzet and Nurija who came to see the president of the War Presidency of Srebrenica municipality, Mr. Avdic, and brought him their reports. I saw them often, because my office was right there, and very often we would attend the morning briefing together. I would bring in my reports and they would bring in theirs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. And just to be totally clear about this, it's no doubt clear already, but you said earlier the former referring to Mirzet Halilovic what the was a commander of the military police and the latter, and that was Nurija Jusufovic was commander of the civilian police and both were subordinated to Becir Bogilovic. Is it right then that Becir Bogilovic was the chief of Mirzet Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was the superior of both Mirzet Halilovic and Nurija Jusufovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown P42 and again we can place it on the ELMO? For the record I'm just going to read a couple of parts of this. It's Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Srebrenica municipality, War Presidency. Srebrenica, 1st July 1992. "On 1 July 1992, pursuant to the decision of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina to declare a state of war, at the initiative of the armed forces and citizens of the free territory of Srebrenica, and in order to fight as successfully as possible against the aggressor, against Bosnia-Herzegovina, the following was adopted in Srebrenica. Decision: To form and appoint members of a War Presidency of Srebrenica municipality." And then "Article 1, the War Presidency of Srebrenica municipality is hereby formed. Article 2: The War Presidency is the most senior organ of government on the free territory of Srebrenica and has all the competencies of the Srebrenica municipal assembly." Now, stopping there, my question is: Was that your understanding, that the War Presidency was the highest organ on the free territory of Srebrenica with all the competencies of the Srebrenica municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The War Presidency was the supreme organ of Srebrenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. I skip Article 3. We can see for ourselves what that says. For Article 4, it says "the following are hereby appointed members of the War Presidency," and there is a list of names, one to 11 which I'm going to come to in a moment. The first -- I want you to turn to the last page and we see that it's signed by the president of the War Presidency, Hajrudin Avdic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So would it be right that Hajrudin Avdic, the president of the War Presidency, was the one who made these appointments?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Going back to Article 4, I want to ask you about some of the people listed there and how often they appeared at the municipal building and attended meetings of the War Presidency in 1992. Firstly, Hajrudin Avdic.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Hajrudin Avdic was there more or less constantly, all the time, in the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Hamdija Fejzic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Hamdija Fejzic was also there often. Resid Efendic, occasionally. Naser sometimes rarely. He was the one I saw least. Dzemal Becirovic was there often. Jusuf Halilovic. I don't know what he did, in some kind of civilian protection that wasn't really functioning. Becir Bogilovic came occasionally, as I said. Instead of him, Mirzet Halilovic and Nurija Jusufovic would come because, I repeat, he had been wounded in the leg and couldn't move around so easily. Mirsad Dudic was on the ground more often. He came rarely. Legic [phoen] Mandzic, Azif Nekic, and Senahid Tabakovic also came in rarely to the Srebrenica municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Just one possible correction. In the English, and it may be the interpreters were looking at the English, it does appear to say Lefik [phoen] Mandzic. Could you confirm, please, that -- well, the name at number 9 in B/C/S? Could you read that name for us, please?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Sefik, Sefik Mandzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now a moment ago, you said that use you've Halilovic you're not sure what he did, some kind of civilian protection, that wasn't really functioning. Do you know why that wasn't functioning or do you have any explanation?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Well, simply the conditions were not in place for civilian protection to function.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And for the War Presidency as a whole, did that in fact function properly in this period, still with July, July August, 1992? Did it function, as far as you could see?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness was not receiving interpretation of the last question, if my friend could repeat the last question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suggest you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was the War Presidency in fact functioning properly, as far as you could see, in July 1992, firstly?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: It could not have functioned in the true sense and, in my opinion, it existed more on paper than in reality. It did not really have the ability to create anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I was asking about July 1992 but the statement you've just made, that it couldn't function, it existed more on paper, is that for any particular time period or is that right through to demilitarisation?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: That is true for the entire period through to demilitarisation because there were no conditions in place to enable it to function properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you know someone called Hakija Meholjic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know whether he took on any function in around spring of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the spring of 1993, he replaced Mr. Becir Bogilovic. He replaced Becir Bogilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Earlier you mentioned Atif Krdzic. Is it correct that in fact it was Hakija Meholjic who replaced Becir Bogilovic then?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Akif Krdzic replaced Mirzet Halilovic at the point when Mirzet Halilovic was replaced, I believe, because Mirzet was removed from the post. I don't know why, whether it was misconduct or something else. I wouldn't wish to go into that, but at any rate, Akif Krdzic replaced Mirzet Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you know who replaced or who removed Mirzet Halilovic from his post, who or what organ?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Mirzet Halilovic was removed by the War Presidency, which had the authority over him and his work.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And finally, then, also for the period that Becir Bogilovic was in his function, you said earlier that that -- he was already in that position in early July 1992. You said he was replaced by Hakija Meholjic which was in the spring of 1993. So can you help us now with what in fact was the periods that Becir Bogilovic was in function as the head of the civilian and military police?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Becir Bogilovic held the position of the chief of the police and civilian police practically through to demilitarisation, because nobody else was appointed to his post except for the stage when Hakija Meholjic arrived. That was the time when the things changed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours I would just wish to enter a correction on the transcript. The witness said the chief of the military and civilian police. I believe this did not enter into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that needs to be corrected. But first let's have a confirmation from the witness himself. In fact, actually, he had stated it earlier on in the day, you know, so I think we can take it for granted and move ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fine. I think I will just ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move because some 30 minutes ago he did precisely state that. So let's move forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Fine, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned this police building, this SUP or MUP building. You've mentioned that that was used both by civilian and military police together. Is it right then that that building was under the jurisdiction of Becir Bogilovic as the head of the military police and the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown P109? Hopefully after the break we'll have -- more of us will have the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Once that has arrived, so don't worry about that. We will find a solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There is just a one page document now. Since not everyone has it in front of them I'll read part of it. It's the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Srebrenica Municipal Territorial Defence Staff, Srebrenica, 2 July 1992. And its subject is "decisions of the Territorial Defence Staff, Srebrenica." It says "At the meeting of the Crisis Staff of Srebrenica TO on 1st July 1992, three decisions were made for solving some of the problems in the current situation on the territory controlled by Srebrenica TO forces. Since the previous War Presidency had left the territory of the municipality, the new War Presidency was formed." And then it mentions the members of the War Presidency. Now, a moment ago you agreed, did you not, that once formed, that body, the War Presidency, was the highest organ on the territory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And would you agree that the last document that we saw was in fact a formal act of appointing members the War Presidency signed by the president of the War Presidency, whereas this is a report on formations and appointments? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And it says, paragraph 3, "A decision was made to form wartime military police, Mirzet Halilovic was appointed the commander of this unit." Now first if you can help with this. In the English translation it says "commander," but in Bosnian it says something else, doesn't it? It says "rukovodilac."

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: That is practically the same. If you have the military hierarchy in mind, then, of course, it would be logical to call him commander. Otherwise, he could be called "rukovodilac", head.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My question is this, really: Is that a normal word to use in this context? Is that the proper term to use?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It can be used, the term.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Commandant or komandir would be more proper?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. If a military formation is involved. However, they had two or three rifles perhaps. To put it simply, this record was done by unprofessionals who didn't know what the military, what the civilian hierarchies were, and, in my opinion, this record has not been done properly. It has been done incompetently.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Now regarding that paragraph, to your knowledge, which organ formed the military police and appointed Mirzet Halilovic as its head?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: No military organ formed the military police. The military police was established by the War Presidency, as I've already indicated. And the War Presidency had the jurisdiction over the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm going to the next paragraph, the next two paragraphs it refers to the formation of a communications and information service. And I think you've already explained that that was also under the War Presidency and that your commission was part of that service. Have I summarised that correctly?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you in fact know Hamed Alic who was apparently appointed the chief of this service?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Where did he work in July 1992 and afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: He worked in the post office building in the Srebrenica municipal -- or, rather, in Srebrenica itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Just to be absolutely clear because it's an important point. The post office building is a separate building from the municipal building, correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: That's right. It's some 400 to 500 metres away from the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was there a room there in which Hamid Alic worked?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would frequent Hamid Alic in his office because, in that period, he was my superior. There was a room there with a radio set over which he kept in touch with Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was there any sort of armed guard outside that room or not?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: No. Why would there be one? I never saw any armed guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you know who if anyone Hamid Alic delivered his reports to?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Solely to the president of the War Presidency, Mr. Hajrudin Avdic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And as far as what was transmitted on the radio, was Hamid Alic able to transmit whatever he liked or did he have to have some approval?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, he had to have an approval. No information was allowed to be transmitted over the radio without either the signature or the written approval of the president of the War Presidency, Mr. Hajrudin Avdic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: I am aware of this because, as I said a minute ago, I went to the post office oftentimes and whenever I had -- something had to be sent over, Hajrudin Avdic [as interpreted], although my superior trusted in me and he would tell me, "I cannot send anything out without Hajrudin Avdic's approval," that is the president of the War Presidency, and that is how I know that he was unable to send out any information without his consent.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, finally, who told you that? I think there might be an error in the transcript. Who told you that he couldn't send anything out without the approval of Hajrudin Avdic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Hamid himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that's a good moment to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones. We will reconvene in 25 minutes' time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may before Mr. Jones gets started I just want to put on the record that with respect to the area in which Defence has been cross-examining -- has been examining this witness, I would ask that there be no leading questions. I did not object previously. There were a few suggestive questions put. I know we are short on time but I'd only ask that counsel not lead in these areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which area because he's been touching on several areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, with respect to the functioning of the different organs and who is in charge and who is subordinated to whom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones, at the same time, at the same time, as we go along, if Mr. Jones touches upon other matters which are not contested by the Prosecution, please stand up and say so because it could spare us -- save us quite a few minutes, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Particularly, for example, when he was dealing with attacks on Glogova, attacks here and attacks there. If you agree that there had been such attacks you just stand up and say we agree there have been such attacks on such and such a day and the rest you can deal with obviously without any interference. But you've got the message now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, may I just say, Your Honour, the principle, of course, is that unless there is a timely objection, then any objection to a leading question is waived. At no time this morning was there an objection from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And so certainly it's not appropriate to say that any questions were suggestive or leading. If they wanted to make that has an objection then they had to do it on time rather than later. I'll take it as an indication --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's ---

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: It is. It is, for the future. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, starting immediately with a new exhibit, and for the record the ERN number is 01787774. And while that's being distributed I'll just read for the record -- after the witness has it. Yes, it says "Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, War Presidency of the Municipal Staff of the armed forces, communications and information service, Srebrenica 2 August 1992," and then I move down to "the approval is hereby granted to Nijaz Masic to take statements from persons who have reliable information about the genocide perpetrated by the occupier against Muslims, Croats, and other ethnic groups." And then it's signed for the communications service.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My question is this, Mr. Sacirovic. You told us before the break that the communications and information service was under the War Presidency. Does this document confirm that or not?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in this document, it appears Nijaz Masic is being tasked to investigate genocide committed against various ethnic groups. My question is, did you ever receive a similar approval?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did. However, my approval and the decision on my appointment was signed by the president of the War Presidency, Hajrudin Avdic, and not by Hamed Alic, as is the case here for this particular gentleman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. When we have documents please make sure that the English version is put on the ELMO because members of the public and others outside following the proceedings that need, or rather have a right to be able to follow properly. All right? Thank you. So let's put this document on the ELMO for a brief moment. Sorry to have interrupted you, Mr. Jones, but I think it's important.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In the meantime I might just ask the following.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead. I mean it's -- I just want to show it to the public, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In terms of the decision on your appointment signed by Hajrudin Avdic, do you know happened to that document? Do you still have it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't have the document. All these documents stayed behind in Srebrenica. I don't have it here with me and I cannot show it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Stayed behind in Srebrenica? When?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: On the 11th of July 1995 when Srebrenica was occupied.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what was your mandate, which you received from Hajrudin Avdic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: My mandate was to hold the position of the president of the commission for the gathering of facts about the war crimes committed in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was that concerned only with war crimes committed against Muslims or was it for any ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Not only did it involve Muslims but all the inhabitants regardless of their religion or ethnicity. We gathered whatever information we were able to gather, given the terrain itself and the access we had to it. So we gathered information about all the crimes committed, regardless of the victims, because when we talk about the crimes, one should not pay attention to one's creed, race or ethnicity. So we investigated into all the crimes committed against members of all the different ethnicities and religions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you did so on behalf of and with a mandate from the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd ask for an exhibit number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Jones. What's the next number, please? 800.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D862, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 862. So this document which consists of two pages, one B/C/S, one in English, with ERN 01787774, is being tendered and marked as Defence Exhibit D862.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And we have the next exhibit, there will be a sequence of exhibits now. It's ERN number is 01787792. And just as that's being handed to the witness for the record I'll read at the top. It says, "Communications and reporting" -- well, in English reporting service. In Bosnian it appears to say "information service." I'll ask the witness about that. The date, "Srebrenica, 5 August 1992, entry permit for Sabahudin Gluhic and Edhem Vranjkovina in order to film the damage caused to the factory in Zeleni Jadar."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: First, could you read at the top, the service which is referred to there? Yes [B/C/S spoken]. Do you see that at the top?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is that the service which you spoke about before the break, headed by Hamed Alic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, do you know either or both of Sabahudin Gluhic or Edhem Vranjkovina?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: I know both of them. They were members of my team. They were my subordinates, according to a hierarchy. Sabahudin Lukic [phoen] was a cameraman. He was the one filming and Edhem Vranjkovina was there with me also, and we were together gathering information about the war crimes committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you work from an office at any point, your team?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is that the office you referred to earlier in the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the same office in the municipal building on the second floor, in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can I ask for an exhibit number for this document, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Can you tell us who signed this, if possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, can you give the document back to him for a moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you help us with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was going to put the same question myself also with regard to the previous document, D862. If he can recognise both or either of those two signatures.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This signature here does not really seem familiar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. Let me just take a look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are talking of D863.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot remember. I cannot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No problem. Usher, can you please show him also the previous document, D862, and see whether he recognises that signature? And if you don't recognise it, unless you are sure, Mr. Sacirovic, don't --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. This signature is familiar to me. It's the signature of Hamed Alic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, thank you very much, Your Honour. And I think for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We haven't give it a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this last document that has been made use of by the Defence consisted of two pages, one B/C/S, one in English, with ERN number 01787792, is being tendered and received and marked as Defence Exhibit D863.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And we have another exhibit which is ERN number 01787791. Which is the prior ERN number to the document we just exhibited. And since it's short I'll just read now into the record. It says, "Report. We have successfully prepared and gathered information from the Zeleni Jadar area."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, do you see that document, Mr. Sacirovic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you see who signed it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Sabahudin Gluhic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you recall an information-gathering exercise undertaken by your team in Zeleni Jadar?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A factory had been shelled and badly damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is this the report relating to the entry permit which we just saw a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll just ask for an exhibit number for this document, too, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document which also consists of two pages, the one in B/C/S handwritten and the other one consisting in the English translation thereof and in a typed format, is being tendered, received, and marked as Defence Exhibit D864.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And then three more exhibits, first D266. This is already a Defence Exhibit. Since it's short I'll just read the following: "Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, municipal War Presidency, dated 16 August 1992, order, the employees Edhem Vranjkovina and Sabahudin Gluhic to go to Suceska local commune on 17 August 1992 in order to make a video recording of the war damage and general situation in the local commune of Suceska." It's signed by Hajrudin Avdic for the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, is it correct to understand this document as the War Presidency ordering members of your commission to collect evidence of war damage in Suceska?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You can see that from the order and from Mr. Avdic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And is this still linked to the collection of evidence of war crimes?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When you found such evidence in 1992, would you report it to the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: We were duty-bound to bring in and hand over any written documents or videotapes. We would hand all those over to the president of the War Presidency. We were duty-bound to do so. It was our obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And that's the same person, is it not, to whom Mirzet Halilovic reported in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All his subordinates brought reports to him. Mirzet Halilovic and Nurija Jusufovic, Becir Bogilovic, myself. Any service over which the War Presidency had competency.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And then we have a new -- another new document which is 01787789. Yes. I have -- there are actually two documents which are in ERN number sequential and it might be better to have them together just to expedite matters. And the first one, 01787789, "Order. Film the interior of the factory in Potocari, Edhem Vranjkovina, and Sabahudin Gluhic will do the filming, War Presidency," and then a signature. Now, does this confirm what you've told us that the War Presidency issued orders to your commission to do filming?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could we have D863, please, shown again, to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm wondering if you could just look at the signature on the document which has just been put in front of you and then the signature which you were asked to look at earlier.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Ah, yes. Yes, now I recall. Yes. This is the signature of the president of the War Presidency of Srebrenica Municipality, Hajrudin Avdic. Sometimes one has a mental block and I was unable to recognise it but I do recognise it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And then the next document, 01787790 which we are tendering together, this is report from the cameraman and director team, "team consisting of a cameraman and director was supposed to go to Potocari as ordered to film the interior of the factory there. However, the task was not carried out as that area was being heavily shelled by Chetniks from Bratunac." And then, can you tell us there who appears to have signed this document?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: At the bottom of this document are the signatures of Mr. Edhem Vranjkovina and Sabahudin Gluhic, the cameraman.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you recall this, this assignment in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I do. I was down there too but you couldn't approach the place. There was no opportunity to go there. There was shelling all day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd ask for an exhibit number for these two documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So these two documents, consisting of two pages in B/C/S with ERN number 01787789 and 01787790, together with the corresponding translation into English on two separate sheets of paper is being tendered, marked, and received as Defence Exhibit D865.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You just mentioned this shelling all day in Potocari. Was that a common or uncommon occurrence in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC
utterances.text: It was common. Potocari was shelled every day. Sometimes more, sometimes less intensely but not a day went by without its being shelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
